text: In South Korea, the government says that having one child earns you 2 million won, which is about 40 million won in our currency.
Hungary goes even further, granting women who have four or more children a lifetime exemption from personal income tax
Japan has even established an agency dedicated to caring for children and families
Yet, in these countries, the birth rate is still declining
I was reading these statistics and wondering why people still refuse to have children even with money
The normal logic is that they're probably too poor to have children. But now that they have money, they should have more children, right?
People used to have many children even when they were poor
To explain this, we have to go back to the first step of starting a family: dating. And we'll use the theoretical framework of game theory to explain why dating is becoming increasingly difficult
Why are there so many dating apps, yet people are still single
And with this trend of no one getting married or having children, many countries will disappear within 100 years
Welcome to our cat-themed adaptation series. We're adapting great foreign videos into Vietnamese for you to refer to
Actually, we've always done this, but now we're going to do it more officially
And our first series is the game theory series from the Predictive History channel
In this video, we'll base our content on those videos, as well as add our own research and counter-arguments — so we can have more productive meals, sleep, and dish-washing sessions.
Okay, let's begin

First, let's talk a little about game theory. Any game will have three parts: the players, which are the participants; the rules, which are the constraints, the limitations, what can and cannot be done; and the rewards.
Because there must be rewards in a game; no one plays for no reason. It's what makes players want to play

To understand a game, we need to understand who is playing, what the rules are, and what the rewards are. And if we understand those three things, we can guess where the game will go. Scene 3: Simulating a 10-person society
Okay, now let's apply this theoretical framework to the dating story. Now imagine a society with 10 people, five men and five women, and all of them want to date and get married.
These five men will belong to five different social classes and will be ranked from 1 to 5 based on criteria such as appearance, health, wealth, and social status
Number five will be the ultimate catch, while number one will be the lowest.
Instinctively, all women will want to marry number five, and all five men will want to date all five women at the same time.
This is because women want a partner capable of protecting and providing for them, while men want to maximize their fertility, so they want to date many women.
However, if all the women only chase after number five, it won't work
Because the other four men will team up to deal with number five
If number five decides to date all five women at the same time, then number five will realize that number five is no longer the most desirable person
Because this guy is too promiscuous and doesn't guarantee a future, the best option for girl number 5 becomes guy number 4.
At this point, girl number 4 will lose her best option, so she'll have to choose guy number 3
Then girl number 3 will have to marry guy number 2, and girl number 2 will marry guy number 1.
And the result is that guy number 5, the most eager one, ends up stuck with girl number 1
Actually, girl number 3 could still marry guy number 5 — the gap there is smaller. But to simplify, let's just assume the cascade above.
And the final result is that guy number 5, who should have gotten the best outcome, gets the worst one. Every girl ends up worse off — except girl number one. The only upside: every guy benefits.
Actually, this is just a small assumption to illustrate the point: in a game, the strongest person, if too greedy, suffers a bitter end — and their rivals benefit directly.
From this, we can deduce that the strongest person isn't the one who can steal everything from everyone else, but the one who can coordinate so that everyone benefits the most
Because if they just steal, the strongest person might win in the short term, but in the long term, everyone will lose
Because even though Mr. Four gets Ms. Five, there's still a disparity between the two, so conflicts and difficulties will inevitably arise
Therefore, the best solution is cooperation. Mr. Five takes Ms. Five, Mr. Four takes Ms. Four, Mr. Three takes Ms. Three — everyone finds a partner, everyone has children, and society develops.
This state — game theory calls it Nash equilibrium. It's a state where no one benefits by unilaterally changing strategy. Everyone's content, and any change would only bring more losses.
So, let's just keep things as they are. That theory is perfectly fine. But there's a problem: society doesn't have just 10 people — it has 8 billion.
A fun survey asks: if you're 30, your parents are pressuring you, you've dated for 10 years with no luck, and now you're forced to marry someone — what's your minimum requirement?
I think it would be simpler for guys — like, any girl will do, even girl number one.
Some girls say: if I don't love him, or find him attractive, then at least he must be earning around 200 million a month.
According to Nash equilibrium, number three should marry number three and live happily
But in reality, number three looks at number three and thinks: better to stay single, unless I meet a number five or someone earning 200 million a month.
In reality, many people rush into the top 1-2%, and most end up being left behind
For example, Elon Musk, he has a ton of children and many wives. Billionaires and celebrities have no shortage of people lining up for them
Meanwhile, many young people around the world are experiencing involuntary singlehood — they want a partner and want to marry, but can't.
So gradually, they give up. As for the guys — many in their 20s and 30s have never dated, never had a relationship, and don't want to try anymore.
Grandpa, that sounds like me, right
It's not because they're ugly or incompetent, but simply because the dating game is too tiring now — competition is fierce, the odds of winning are low.
That's the theory saying balance is optimal. But in reality, people don't want to play that game anymore. Why? As I said, a game has three parts: the players — that hasn't changed much.
The rules of the game are competition, and that hasn't changed much. Scene 6: The New Reward of the Game
The final thing is the reward. Dating rewards used to mean love, sex, marriage, and children. But now there's another element — one that used to matter, but is now exaggerated: social status.
Simply put, if you love this person and marry this person, can you show them off
Can you be proud in the eyes of others? Show them off on Facebook, on Instagram, at a class reunion, bragging about how handsome, rich, hot, or capable your partner is?
Now the story has added an extremely important element: reputation. And it doesn't stop at marriage — it shows up in the latest iPhone, luxury travel, designer goods.
Many people do things not because they use them, but to show off. Marriage is part of this game too: marrying below your standard is embarrassing, so better to stay single.
The scary thing is that the game of showing off is a zero-sum game
That means there will always be people better off and people worse off. If everyone could show off, then no one could.
If there are people at the top, there must be people at the bottom
There's a common view that government cash incentives don't work — because the problem was never a lack of money.
Nowadays, finding a job is easier — there may be a lot of unemployment, but it's easier than in the past, when people only knew farm work. Now there are more choices.
So now, people can find a normal job, stay healthy, and earn enough to live on. But the real thing they lack is face.
And face can't necessarily be bought with money. If you give someone a billion to marry someone their friends look down on, what does that billion even mean?
Actually, it does have meaning — but in the end, some people would rather stay single than marry someone their friends look down on.
Here's a question: if humans always chase this kind of "face", why has our species survived for tens of thousands of years, remaining numerous and never going extinct? The answer is...

From Mr. Giang at the Predictive History channel: humans didn't always behave this way, because the game changes over time. Game theory calls this the overall picture — the big context around the game: population size, whether society is rich or poor, whether there are outside threats, how advanced the technology is.
These factors combine to determine which game is played. When the context changes, the game changes too. Let's divide human history into three stages for easier understanding.
The first stage is the primitive era. A small village had only about 200 people. Everything was scarce and inconvenient — even getting clean water meant carrying it home to boil.
Having children in such circumstances was like stepping into a death trap

In that context, there was no concept of love or dating — men and women had many partners at once, partly to raise everyone's odds of reproducing, and partly so no one knew exactly whose child was whose.
When the men in the village all thought the child might be theirs, everyone would flock together to protect and care for it. And the reward would be ensuring the entire village didn't become extinct
Let's move to the second stage, when the small village grew into a society of tens of thousands, with money changing hands and some rudimentary technology.
At this time, villages and tribes began fighting each other constantly over territory and resources — so society became extremely short of people.
Because soldiers were needed for war, and hands were needed in the fields, where would anyone find time for courtship and romantic dates?
And so, arranged marriages took center stage. Parents decided who their children married, with no room for argument — as long as they married and had many children.
And finally, the third stage is the present day. The world is crowded now — 8 billion people. Look at China or India: each has over a billion, very crowded.
And there's much more money too — but some have far more than enough, while others struggle to get by. Very unequal.
The upside is that healthcare is better and technology is more advanced, so mothers who give birth are almost guaranteed to survive — childbirth is no longer a death sentence.
And then, the world is relatively peaceful, in a certain way — superpowers no longer shoot each other directly, they wage proxy wars instead.
Talk aside, life is genuinely much better now. But because life is better, people expect dating to be good too.
While dating, falling in love, and marriage — like everything else — must have both good and bad sides.
So if you're going to endure hardship anyway, why date someone from your own class and suffer together? Why not aim for someone from a higher class instead?
So now, dating is pretty much a jump-starting platform. Lower levels try to climb to higher ones.
Apps like Tinder, Bumble, or dating groups on Facebook are essentially platforms for finding a better match to jump to.
But the problem is: if everyone wants to jump to a higher level, who wants to marry someone at their own level? If you're a 3 wanting a 5, or at best a 4 — why settle for another 3?
So, marriage and childbirth are plummeting

And Mr. Giang says that if this trend continues, society will collapse sooner or later — and history has already proven it. The clearest sign of a collapsing civilization is when educated, wealthy women start refusing to have children.
He says: "Really? I don't know about that." Don't take it as looking down on women — I love women very much.
Although — in part — the Roman Empire, when it collapsed, faced the same scenario.
The Romans at that time were both rich and skilled — so they decided not to have children, or to have very few.
And the situation became so serious that Emperor Augustus enacted the Lex Iulia — punishing those too lazy to marry, and rewarding those with many children.
That means more than 2000 years ago, people tried using money and policies to solve the problem. But the results were not very effective
Rome still collapsed as usual, though. This wasn't the only reason — just one part of the story.
Speaking of collapse, let's look at the numbers. The replacement birth rate is 2.1 children per woman — below that, we start seeing a shortage of people.
Below 1.5, the decline is rapid. Below 1.0, society is essentially self-destructing.
Looking at the world map, we see it's split into two states: in Africa, birth rates are still very high — some regions average five to seven children per mother.
Because there, they are still in the stage where they need people to survive and then fight for territory and things like that, so they just have as many children as possible to compensate

Meanwhile, in the wealthy regions of North America, Europe, and East Asia, the birth rate is plummeting. In North America and Europe, there are still immigrants — if native women don't want children, so be it.
They open their doors to foreigners to work, pay taxes, and contribute to the economy — though it also stirs up cultural and political headaches, a hot topic in Europe and America.
And in East Asia, we're really sitting on a powder keg. Scene 11: South Korea
Because here, there's no easily opening the doors to immigrants — East Asian culture is fairly closed, and it's hard to accept strangers at the same table.

South Korea is a prime example: their birth rate has dropped to around 0.6-0.8, the lowest in the world. At this rate, Korea will likely survive only a few more generations before disappearing from the map.
Now, there are even restaurants with "No Kid Zone" signs — treating children as a noisy nuisance ruining other customers' experience.

According to Mr. Giang, South Korea is like this because it's a society that values appearance to an extreme degree — everything has to be beautiful, high-quality, and expensive. Look at Korean showbiz: idols, actors, everyone has to be perfectly beautiful.
But where do idols and shows come from? And usually, people in Korea are also caught up in this "perfection trap." And because of that, the path to success there is quite narrow

Either you get into a prestigious university and work for Samsung or another major corporation, or you have no decent options at all. So if you're a middle-class family in Korea, you'll hear this argument:

If you have three children, you need more than three times the money and resources. If none can get into a top school, just pour everything into one and send them to extra classes from dawn to night, hoping they'll pass and change their family's life.
And this logic forces people to have only one child — or none at all — just to avoid the burden.

Currently, Korea's population seems relatively stable, since the working-age group is still fairly large — but around 2040, the imbalance begins: the elderly population will skyrocket while children keep shrinking.
By 2060, the workforce will be halved. No one to work, no one to serve in the military.
So, a society of just old folks sitting in parks with no one creating wealth only leads to a national economic collapse.
China is the same. Its birth rate is now only about 1.0...
...whereas five years ago it was still 1.7 — now it's plummeting.
At this rate, by the end of the century, China's population will likely be halved — around 600 million.
Actually, 600 million is still a lot — but with so many elderly people, the system won't be able to support itself.

Speaking of birth rates, there's an interesting comparison: usually, the richer a country, the fewer children it has. But there are exceptions — this country is rich and advanced, yet families still have more than two children.
So, using game theory: Israel's reward is different, shaped by history and religion. Having children there is tied to community and national identity — a source of pride, not a burden.
In oil-rich countries too, people still have many children — the state covers everything from healthcare to housing, and religion encourages having more.
You might ask if this model survives once the oil runs out. Only the future will tell.
The key point, from a game theory perspective: societies where having children enhances prestige will have high birth rates.
Conversely, if having children means losing freedom, money, time, and career opportunities, people choose not to. So — what about Vietnam?
In 2024, Vietnam's birth rate fell to 1.91 per woman, the lowest in our history — the third year in a row below 2.1.
The downward trend is very clear. We lose a little each year — and 2024 was even the Year of the Dragon, a year our culture considers auspicious for having children.
But even with such strong spiritual beliefs, they can't beat the modern game of saving face — thinking about the cost, fatigue, and career impact, people just give up on having children.
In big cities, the birth rate is only 1.67. Rural areas are slightly higher but also declining. Ho Chi Minh City has the country's lowest, at just 1.39 — and the age of first marriage keeps rising.
Men now have to be around 30 to get married, and women around 25
This aligns well with the framework: the more educated and wealthy people are, the fewer children they have — too much to lose by having them.
Many experts predict that if this continues, after 2035 Vietnam's population will start shrinking — deaths outpacing births. Seven provinces already show early signs of this.
Although Vietnam isn't as dire as South Korea or China yet, we're on the same path, and heavily influenced by social media.
In the old days, people lived in a small village or neighborhood of only a few hundred people. They only compared themselves to those around them.
The odds of being the top person in your small neighborhood were fairly high, so people happily married so their children could live well, comfortably above the local average.
Now it's completely different
On TikTok, you see guys with six-pack abs driving Porsches; on Instagram, girls with perfect skin carrying designer bags. Anyone successful is now known to the whole of society.
So, naturally, you start comparing yourself to millions of people online
And then, the people around you don't seem good enough anymore. Social media expanded the playing field from a few hundred people to millions, pushing standards up unreasonably.
Dating apps are the same: swiping through hundreds of people a day tricks your brain into thinking you have too many choices.
There's no need to rush, you think — keep swiping, better people will come. The result: you end up choosing no one, or not liking anyone even when you do meet up.
From a game theory perspective, social media has multiplied the number of players a thousandfold, while the prizes at the top stay the same — the odds of winning are practically zero.
But people still play, because they see everyone else still playing.
Actually, after watching the source video and writing this script, we realized game theory doesn't hand you an answer right away — it only teaches you how to ask the right question.
For any situation, ask yourself: who are the players, what are the rules, and what's the reward? From there, you can see the bigger picture — where things stand, and where they're headed.
Dating is just one example. This same framework applies to the US-Iran tension, the war in Ukraine, or why this could be Vietnam's moment to break through.
Okay, that's enough for now, let's stop here. What do you think — is the game of saving face affecting your own dating and marriage decisions? Or is it something else? Let us know in the comments.
